summary: Magnesium is an essential mineral and major intracellular cation required for hundreds of enzymatic reactions, neuromuscular function, and cardiac rhythm. As an over-the-counter supplement it is supplied as various salts (oxide, citrate, chloride, sulfate, hydroxide) for dietary supplementation and correction of hypomagnesemia; magnesium oxide/hydroxide also act as antacids and osmotic laxatives, and intravenous magnesium sulfate is used for eclampsia, severe asthma, and torsades de pointes. The adult RDA is roughly 310-420 mg of elemental magnesium per day, and supplemental doses vary by salt and elemental content. The major safety concern is hypermagnesemia, which is chiefly a risk in renal impairment; diarrhea is the dose-limiting effect of oral magnesium salts.
indications: Dietary supplementation as a source of the essential mineral magnesium
Magnesium oxide/hydroxide as an antacid and as an osmotic (saline) laxative
IV magnesium sulfate for eclampsia/pre-eclampsia, severe acute asthma, and torsades de pointes (parenteral, specialist use)

moa: Magnesium is an essential cofactor for over 300 enzymatic reactions, including those involving ATP, and is critical for nucleic acid and protein synthesis, neuromuscular transmission, and cardiac and smooth muscle function. As an electrolyte supplement it replaces or augments body magnesium stores. Poorly absorbed magnesium salts (oxide, hydroxide, sulfate, citrate) retain water in the gut osmotically, producing a laxative effect, while magnesium oxide/hydroxide also neutralize gastric acid as antacids. Pharmacologically, magnesium has membrane-stabilizing and calcium-antagonist properties used in conditions such as eclampsia and torsades de pointes.

absolute: Severe renal failure / marked renal impairment (risk of hypermagnesemia)
Known hypersensitivity to the magnesium product or excipients
Heart block (for parenteral magnesium) unless specifically indicated and monitored
relative: Mild to moderate renal impairment (dose-reduce and monitor)
Myasthenia gravis (magnesium can worsen neuromuscular weakness)
Bowel obstruction or acute abdomen (for laxative use)
monitor: Deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, and blood pressure with IV/high-dose use

preg: Magnesium is an essential mineral with an established recommended intake in pregnancy, and dietary/supplemental intake within recommended amounts is generally considered acceptable. IV magnesium sulfate is used therapeutically in pregnancy (e.g., eclampsia) under specialist care. Follow professional guidance for doses beyond normal dietary supplementation.
lact: Magnesium is a normal constituent of breast milk. Usual supplemental and dietary intake is considered compatible with breastfeeding; high-dose or parenteral use should follow clinical guidance.
renal: The kidneys are the main route of magnesium excretion, so renal impairment is the major risk factor for hypermagnesemia. Use magnesium supplements with caution and at reduced doses in mild to moderate renal impairment, and avoid them in significant chronic kidney disease or renal failure. Monitor serum magnesium and watch for signs of hypermagnesemia (hypotension, loss of deep tendon reflexes/areflexia, respiratory depression, and in severe cases cardiac arrest).
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment for the mineral supplement. Standard precautions apply.

major: Reduces absorption of oral tetracyclines (separate dosing by several hours)
Reduces absorption of oral fluoroquinolones (separate dosing by several hours)
Reduces absorption of oral bisphosphonates (separate dosing by several hours)
moderate: Other agents/conditions that raise magnesium in renal impairment (additive hypermagnesemia)
Neuromuscular blocking agents (magnesium can potentiate blockade)
Calcium channel blockers (additive hypotension with IV magnesium)
minor: Antacid/laxative overuse altering bowel function and electrolyte balance
interactions.food: Taking with food may reduce GI upset; magnesium is naturally present in foods (green leafy vegetables, nuts, whole grains, legumes)
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use commonly causes magnesium depletion; no direct interaction with the supplement itself
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum magnesium; high doses can affect serum calcium and potassium handling

rare: Flushing and lethargy with high serum levels
emergency: Severe hypermagnesemia: profound hypotension, areflexia, respiratory depression, and cardiac arrest - medical emergency treated with IV calcium

monitoring: Serum magnesium, particularly in renal impairment or with IV/high-dose use
Deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, and blood pressure during IV or high-dose therapy
Bowel habit and hydration with laxative use
counsel: This is a mineral supplement and electrolyte, not an FDA-approved prescription drug at usual supplemental doses
If you have kidney disease, talk to your clinician before taking magnesium - it can build up to dangerous levels
Loose stools or diarrhea are common; lower the dose or take with food if this happens
Separate magnesium from certain antibiotics (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones) and from bisphosphonate bone medicines by a few hours
Seek medical help for severe weakness, very low blood pressure, slow or shallow breathing, or feeling faint
pk: Oral laxative effect typically within ~30 minutes to 6 hours; supplementation corrects deficiency over days
Serum magnesium rises within hours of oral dosing; IV magnesium acts within minutes
Regulated mainly by renal excretion; no fixed half-life - elimination is prolonged in renal impairment
Depends on dose, salt, and renal function; effects persist longer when renal clearance is reduced
Store at room temperature in a tightly closed container; keep out of reach of children
pearls: Magnesium is a mineral supplement and electrolyte (essential mineral), not an FDA-approved prescription drug at usual supplemental doses
Hypermagnesemia is the major risk and is chiefly seen in renal impairment, since the kidneys are the main route of magnesium elimination
Hypermagnesemia signs: hypotension, loss of deep tendon reflexes (areflexia), respiratory depression, and cardiac arrest - treated acutely with IV calcium
Diarrhea is the dose-limiting effect of oral magnesium salts; poorly absorbed salts (oxide, citrate, sulfate, hydroxide) also act as osmotic laxatives
Oral magnesium reduces absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and bisphosphonates - separate the doses by several hours
missed: For routine supplementation, take a missed dose when remembered, or skip it if it is nearly time for the next dose. Do not take a double dose to catch up.
overdose: Excessive magnesium causes hypermagnesemia, the major toxicity, particularly when renal function is impaired. Early features include nausea, flushing, and lethargy; worsening levels cause hypotension, loss of deep tendon reflexes (areflexia), respiratory depression, bradycardia/conduction block, and ultimately cardiac arrest. Management: stop all magnesium, support airway/breathing and circulation, give intravenous calcium (e.g., calcium gluconate) to antagonize cardiac and neuromuscular effects, ensure hydration and renal excretion, and use dialysis in severe cases or renal failure.
